extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, and students of poetics composing tragic drama
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing classical tragedy: selecting plot, characters, recognitions, and structuring action to produce pity and fear. Covers plot types (simple/complex), peripeteia and recognition, character-moral requirements, chorus/parts, and stylistic/structural do's and don'ts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of story over versification
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet ought to be esteemed such rather from his story than from his versification, inasmuch as he is a poet by imitation, and he imitates actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the poet chiefly by the quality and arrangement of actions (the story) rather than by metrical skill or ornament; the poet 'gives to his hero certain passions and qualities, and makes him perform certain actions' and thereby instructs morally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry treats universals; history particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry treats more of general principles; history, of particular actions. A general principle is that which a man of a certain character would say or do, according either to probability or necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or composing, favor scenes and actions that reveal universal human types and causes (what a certain character would do) over mere chronicle of unique events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid episodic (unconnected) stories
rubrics_metrics.description: An episodic story is one in which it is neither probable nor necessary that the episodes introduced should follow another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reprobate insertion of anecdotes/adventures that have no reference to the main plot. Episodes introduced for length or prizes that interrupt the connection weaken the tragedy; ensure each episode follows necessarily or probably from the preceding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy should imitate a perfect action that excites pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is the imitation, not only of a perfect action, but of such as excites pity and fear; the feelings to be excited by tragedy are principally fear and pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose a single, coherent action (an 'entire and perfect action') shaped to arouse pity and fear in the audience; the emotional effect should arise from the plot's internal logic and surprises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer complex plots (with peripeteia and recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some stories are simple, others complex. A complex is one in which the change takes place with recognition, or peripeteia, or both; the composition of the best tragedy must be complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design plots that include a reversal (peripeteia) and/or a recognition so that the change in fortune follows necessarily or probably from prior actions; complex plots are artistically superior to simple, linear sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia must arise necessarily or probably from prior actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The peripeteia is the change of actions to their very opposites; this either according to probable, or necessary consequence. Peripeties ought to be the consequence of something gone before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure reversals are organic—caused by earlier events or character choices—rather than accidental; arbitrariness undermines credibility and the emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition should produce decisive change (ideally simultaneous with peripeteia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is a change from ignorance to knowledge, tending to establish either friendship or animosity, and the best kind of recognition is when the peripeteia takes place at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for recognitions that immediately alter the circumstances of the story (rush from happiness to misery or vice versa) and that are central to the action. Recognitions that do not effect love or hatred or substantial change fail their purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include 'passion' as action-producing death or pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Passion is an action productive of death or pain, such as murders openly perpetrated, tortures, wounds, and such like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing tragic incidents, use passions (brutal acts, suffering) that are relevant to the action and emotionally potent; the audience must be clearly informed of such outcomes even if not shown on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts and divisions of tragedy (structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is divided into prologue, episode, exode, and chorus; the chorus itself has parodus and stasimon (parodus = first speech of the whole chorus; stasimon = song without anapaest or trochaeus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure a tragedy with these formal parts in mind; understand the chorus' changing role (initially lighter meter, then grave stasima) and how prologue/episode/exode function in relation to the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select proper moral status of the protagonist (neither very good nor very bad)
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither very just men should be represented as falling from good fortune into bad, nor the wicked from bad fortune into good. The proper tragic man is one 'between the two'—a man in high esteem who falls through some mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a protagonist who is neither entirely virtuous nor deeply wicked; their misfortune should stem from error (hamartia) or frailty rather than vice, to elicit pity and fear rather than indignation or mere pleasure at their fall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer downfall by error (hamartia) from good to bad
rubrics_metrics.description: The change should be from good to bad — by no crime, but by a great mistake of such a man as has been mentioned. The finest tragedy is founded on a story of this nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose the catastrophe so that the hero's misstep (not malicious crime) precipitates the reversal; an ending unhappy through deserved vice does not produce the tragic catharsis desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek incidents among friends/relations to maximize pity
rubrics_metrics.description: When actions which excite passion are committed among friends (e.g., a son killing a father, a brother a brother), these are the incidents to be sought for, because they excite pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer intimate, family-related conflicts and mistaken harms between close relations rather than conflicts among enemies or indifferent parties, which arouse less pity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on monstrous stage effects to produce terror
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who produce by the assistance of stage effect not the terrible, but the monstrous only, have nothing in common with tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid substituting spectacle or bizarre supernatural appearances for genuine plot-driven terror; the aim is pity and fear elicited by human actions and causal reversals, not mere shock or monstrosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Events must follow from necessity or probability; avoid causeless incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: It is requisite to aim at either the necessary or the probable, so that it be necessary or probable that such and such a man say or do such and such things... Nothing done upon the stage should appear to be without a cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure every on-stage action has an intelligible motive and causal antecedent. If something lacks an apparent cause, it should be attributed to events prior to the play's beginning or left out of the representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted use of machinery only for off-stage pre/post events
rubrics_metrics.description: Machinery may be employed in matters out of the drama, either such as happened before it, which a man cannot know, or such as are to follow, which require relation and description; for we attribute to the Gods the power of seeing all things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve deus ex machina and similar devices for reporting or connecting off-stage events that cannot be credibly dramatized in-scene; avoid using them to resolve the central internal logic of the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer peripeteia-based recognition over mark-based or poet-invented tokens
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition by marks (scars, tokens) has less to do with art; those recognitions which proceed from peripeteia are better. Poet-invented recognitions are without art and approach error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When scripting recognition scenes, favor revelations that arise naturally from the plot's development (peripeteia) rather than contrived tokens or arbitrary devices the poet inserts merely to produce recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character manners must be useful, becoming, like, and equal
rubrics_metrics.description: Respecting manners there are four things which the poet ought to attend to: one, that they be useful (show disposition); secondly, that they be becoming; thirdly, that they be like; and fourthly, that they be equal (consistent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design character behavior to reveal inner disposition (useful), to suit social/gender roles (becoming), to match expected likeness or reputation (like), and to remain consistent across the piece (equal). Avoid incongruous shifts in manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in depiction: imitate best traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Since tragedy is an imitation of better men, we ought to copy good portrait painters; preserving the peculiarity of shape and making the portrait like, paint them handsomer than the originals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing characters with rough or negative traits, soften extremes—present a moderated version that preserves recognizability but enhances nobility where appropriate; avoid exaggerated caricature that undermines tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not alter the great traditional occurrences that define a story
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not right to alter traditionary stories (e.g., Clytemnestra dying by the hand of Orestes); the poet ought to invent and use with propriety those which are handed down, but not change the great occurrence upon which the whole story turns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect central canonical facts that anchor a mythic or traditional story's tragic power; you may invent motives or prior adventures, but avoid changing the pivotal event that gives the plot its necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ranking of recognition/act sequences (dramatic effectiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: That which represents a person who knows what he is doing as meditating and not performing an action is the worst; next worst is that he complete the action; it is better that the person should perform an action in ignorance and make the discovery after he has done it; the best is when he is about to do it and recognises (and so does not do it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer dramatic situations where recognition prevents the deed (greatest astonishment and least detestation); avoid creating characters who merely intend crime without consequence or who commit crimes knowingly without tragic pathos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for catharsis: tragedy should purify passions via pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: These maxims support Aristotle's theory that tragedy ought to purify our passions by means of pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the success of a tragedy by its capacity to move and then purify the audience's emotions through well-earned pity and fear produced by the plot and characters' fates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making manners/incidents incongruous with earlier representation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the manner of the person represented be in reality variable and uncertain, we must make it equally so in representation, but as we begin so must we end. Thus if a man be represented as very brave at the commencement of a piece, it will not do to make a coward of him towards the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain internal consistency: do not shift a character's portrayed manner or status in ways unsupported by plot development; any variability must be set up and resolved coherently.
